summary_html: Child safely **reunified with parent or guardian**, case closed. Federal policy treats reunification as the preferred outcome once risk factors are mitigated.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — establishes reunification timelines and permanency goals  
- **SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — funds reunification services and tracks permanency outcomes

primary_citations.citation_text: District of Columbia - D.C. Code § 16-2320 (Disposition of child who is neglected, delinquent, or in need of supervision)
District of Columbia - D.C. Code § 16-2353 (Grounds for termination of parent and child relationship)
District of Columbia - D.C. Code § 4-1303.71 (Definitions — “Youth” means an individual under 21 years of age who is in the care of the Agency)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: Reasonable efforts require CFSA to identify the barriers to reunification and to refer the parent to appropriate services addressing them; CFSA satisfied that duty here and the change of permanency goal from reunification to adoption was affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: It sets out the three-part showing the government must make before abandoning reunification as the goal.
key_cases.quote: requires the District to identify the barriers to reunification and prepare a case plan by recommending appropriate services designed to address the needs of each child and family

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: Sitting en banc the court overruled In re K.M.T. and held that an order changing a neglected child's permanency goal from reunification to adoption is an immediately appealable final order, that permanency goal review hearings must protect parental due process, that the court must first find by a preponderance that the government made reasonable efforts toward reunification, and that a finding of parental unfitness must precede termination absent truly exceptional circumstances or stipulation.
key_cases.relevance: It makes the abandonment of reunification a discrete, appealable decision that the government must justify with proof of reasonable efforts.
key_cases.quote: a change of the presumptive goal of a neglect proceeding from reunification to adoption is an appealable final order

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: The ADA and the Rehabilitation Act protect parents with disabilities from discriminatory curtailment of parental rights and require reasonable accommodations, but the trial court did not violate them where the intellectually disabled mother received extensive services and still could not safely parent, so the goal change to adoption was affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: It is the D.C. authority on when a disabled parent's failure to progress may lawfully end reunification efforts.
key_cases.quote: The ADA and the Rehabilitation Act do protect parents with disabilities, including intellectual and psychiatric disabilities, from discriminatory curtailment of their parental rights.

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: Before terminating parental rights or granting a contested adoption the trial court must expressly determine whether the evidence shows parental unfitness or exceptional circumstances making continuation of the relationship detrimental to the child; because the magistrate judge never articulated that determination the case was remanded.
key_cases.relevance: It recognizes that termination may be inappropriate where a parent's unfitness at the time of trial is reasonably likely to be temporary.
key_cases.quote: a natural parent’s unfitness may be evidenced by a variety of behaviors, conditions, and circumstances, including but not limited to past or ongoing child abuse, neglect, maltreatment, or abandonment

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the suspension of visitation, the change of permanency goal to adoption and the termination of parental rights, holding that the agency's case plan and reasonable efforts were adequate where the mother herself refused to participate in case planning and in the mental health services offered to her.
key_cases.relevance: It is the necessary counterweight at the reunification node: a parent's own non-cooperation can supply the reasonable-efforts finding that permits the District to abandon reunification.
key_cases.quote: She cannot now argue, well after the fact, that the Agency should have done even more than it already did to overcome her uncooperativeness.

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed retention of adoption as the children's sole permanency goal, holding that the case plan was appropriate and reasonable even though the mother never signed the plan documents and the later plan assigned no action components to the agency, and that the reasonable-efforts and inadequate-progress findings were supported by the record.
key_cases.relevance: It is cited alongside In re K.C. for the proposition that a parent's refusal to cooperate bears on whether the government made the reasonable efforts required before reunification is abandoned.
key_cases.quote: Thus, the case plan mirrored what the magistrate judge had ordered; it did not set out requirements that became effective only upon the Mother's signature.

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Must file TPR or document compelling reason
